# Method

In this chapter the approach of this study is described. To answer the
research question, we performed an experiment to record data. A human
is sitting in front of a plant watching a video consisting of a lot of
short video clips to stimulate different emotions. The plant's voltage
signals and the human's HRV data are recorded as well as CO~2~ data. The
human's face is filmed during the experiment, which is used to label its
emotion. This is used as input for the training of the machine learning
models. CO~2~ is also recorded in order to search for correlations as a
basis for future research.

## Architecture Overview

In this section, the system architecture is described. It is organized
as a sequential data pipeline that transforms raw multimodal sensor
recordings into a trained plant-based emotion classifier, and is
complemented by a separate real-time inference component, a Live
Dashboard. @fig-pipeline provides an overview of this pipeline. The
pipeline is split into five main parts: Sensing, Experiment, Labeling,
Features, and ML Models. Each one will be explained in detail in the
following sections. Additionally, this chapter includes a short
description of the Live Demonstration and the CO~2~ correlation
analysis. We manage the code via GitHub. The respective notebooks will be
referred to.

![Overview of the system pipeline.](figures/pipeline.png){#fig-pipeline width=90%}

The first step in the pipeline is sensing, referring to the sensor setup
used to measure the data. Recording is handled by the notebook
`01_init_recording.ipynb`. The setup and the corresponding code are
based on the implementation by Peter Gloor [@gloor2025]. The respective
implementation details are also available in the associated GitHub
repository. We measure the data using the following sensors: plant
electrodes record the plant bioelectric voltage, a camera records the
facial expressions, Polar H10 records HRV and heart rate, and SCD41
records CO~2~. Note that these four physical sensors yield five distinct
data streams, since the Polar H10 provides both heart rate and HRV from
the same chest strap; this is why Section 4.3 refers to five sensor
streams captured throughout each session, despite only four sensors
being physically involved. None of the four sensors acts as a master
clock; instead, all readings are aligned after the fact into one shared
event log, a process described in detail in Section 4.3. The resulting
session, including one event log plus one video file, is the raw data
used in all subsequent steps.

The second step in the pipeline is the experiment. Each session begins
with a participant watching a sequence of short emotion-eliciting video
clips, while five sensor streams are captured alongside: plant
bioelectric voltage, ambient CO~2~, HR, HRV, and facial expressions. The
four sensors run independently. This is further described in
Section 4.3.

The third step in the pipeline is labeling. The notebook
`02_emotion_labelling.ipynb` turns these raw streams into a proxy
emotion label for each 30-second window; this length is chosen on the
basis of ultra-short-term HRV research. Valence and arousal are read from
two separate signals: facial expression and HRV. The facial expressions
are converted into valence using HSEmotion. The HRV is used for arousal.
The result is a five-class label. This is further described in
Section 4.4.

The fourth step in the pipeline is feature engineering: the notebook
`03_dataset_creation.ipynb` runs the labeling pipeline over every
recorded session and merges the results into a single consolidated
dataset, which is later used to train the ML models. This is further
described in Section 4.5.

The fifth step in the pipeline is the training and testing of the ML
models. The notebooks `04_01_ml_pipeline_*.ipynb`,
`04_02_ml_pipeline_*.ipynb`, and `04_03_ml_pipeline_*.ipynb` train and
compare three classifiers: Random Forest, XGBoost, and a neural network
are evaluated separately for emotion, arousal, and valence. The input is
restricted to plant-bioelectric features. This is further described in
Section 4.6.

Additionally to the pipeline, the notebook
`05_Correlation_Analysis.ipynb` includes the CO~2~ correlation analysis.
It follows up on one specific concern raised by the valence result:
could ambient CO~2~, rather than the plant itself, explain why the plant
signal tracks valence? It tests this by checking whether the plant
signal correlates with CO~2~ and CO~2~ with valence, and whether the
plant-valence link survives once CO~2~ is statistically held constant.
This is further described in Section 4.8.

Finally, the trained models are reused outside this batch pipeline in
`phaenomena/emotion_live_dashboard.py`, which infers emotion in real time
as a session takes place. Since the offline normalization above needs an
entire session's data before it can run, the live dashboard uses a
causal variant instead, normalizing each window only against windows
that came before it. This is further described in Section 4.7.

## Sensor Setup

As introduced in Section 4.1, the sensing stage of the pipeline relies
on four independent sensors: plant electrodes, a camera, the Polar H10,
and the SCD41 CO~2~ sensor. This section describes the hardware behind
each of them in more detail, starting with the plant sensing setup
itself.

The plant sensing hardware builds on the ESP32 and AD8232 architecture
used in the Silent Signals project by Gloor's group for the Phänomena
science exhibition in Zurich. The AD8232, originally designed as a heart
rate front end, is repurposed here to amplify the weak bioelectric
signal of the plant. The ESP32 microcontroller reads the amplified
signal and streams it over WebSocket at a rate of 100 Hz. This part of
the setup was adopted directly, while the recording pipeline itself,
described in Section 4.3, was built separately for this project.

A single *Kalanchoe* plant was used throughout all recording sessions.
Three standard medical electrodes, of the same type used for ECG
recordings, were attached using their adhesive surface to the three
largest leaves of the plant. Each electrode was connected to the AD8232
board, which forwarded the resulting voltage signal to the ESP32 for
transmission.

In addition to the plant voltage, the ESP32 also measures an SCD41
sensor, which reports ambient CO~2~ concentration in ppm. CO~2~ is not
sampled at a fixed rate but logged once per received data batch. Two
further sensors complete the setup: a Polar H10 chest strap, connected
via Bluetooth Low Energy, providing R-R intervals for the later
HRV-based arousal label, and a standard webcam recording the
participant's face for the FER-based valence label. How the readings
from these four sensors are recorded and subsequently aligned in time is
described in Section 4.3.

The entire sensor setup was assembled and operated in the Digital Lab of
the Cologne Institute for Information Systems.

## Field Work

Recording is orchestrated by `01_init_recording.ipynb`. None of the four
sensors described in Section 4.2 acts as a master clock; instead, each
sensor writes its readings independently into one shared event log,
timestamping every entry against the local system clock of the
recording computer. This design avoids the need for a common hardware
trigger, at the cost of requiring the four streams to be aligned after
the fact rather than during acquisition; how this alignment is
subsequently performed is described in Section 4.4. The output of a
completed session is this shared event log together with the
corresponding video recording, which together form the raw input to
every following processing step.

Participants were recruited from fellow students, personal
acquaintances, and other students unknown to the team beforehand. All
participants were between 20 and 30 years old and from Germany. In
total, 15 participants completed one session each.

The emotional stimulus consisted of a video of approximately ten minutes
in length, reused from an earlier COIN seminar project [@schafer2025].
The video follows a fixed sequence of emotionally contrasting segments,
beginning with light-hearted content such as clips of dogs and a
humorous advertisement, and later introducing material intended to evoke
disgust, shock, and sadness, including scenes of a more graphic and
violent nature. It ends with an extended unsettling sequence that
concludes with a jump scare. All participants viewed the clips in the
same fixed order.

During the session, participants were seated at a table facing the
laptop and asked to watch the video without any additional task.
Participants were informed verbally about the nature of the video,
including the possibility of disturbing or graphic content, and were
asked whether there were any topics they did not want to be confronted
with. Each participant completed the session alone in the room, and the
room was ventilated between sessions.

The laptop running the video and the recording code was placed on the
left, with the participant seated at the table directly in front of it.
The plant with the attached electrodes stood next to the laptop, and the
board containing the ESP32 and the remaining sensors was positioned to
its right.

## Labeling Algorithm

Self-assessment ratings, for instance following the Self-Assessment
Manikin [@bradleylang1994], would provide a direct subjective report
("honest signal") for each window. They were deliberately not used here,
because such ratings may be influenced by conscious or unconscious
response bias and therefore do not serve as an independent ground truth.
Instead, valence and arousal are derived from separate physiological and
behavioral channels, processed independently, and combined in a final
step to form the crossed emotion label.

Before these channels can be processed, the independently timestamped
sensor streams introduced in Section 4.3 must first be brought onto a
common time grid. Each session is divided into 30-second windows based
on elapsed recording time, and every sensor reading is assigned to the
window whose interval contains its timestamp; only once the plant
voltage, facial video, and R-R interval series have been aligned in this
way can values from different sensors within the same window be treated
as referring to the same moment in the session. This window length
follows @baek2015, who show that 30 seconds is the shortest interval
from which HRV metrics can still reliably approximate the much longer
five-minute windows recommended by standard HRV guidelines. These
30-second windows are non-overlapping and form the grid used for
calibration and model training; a denser, overlapping 5-second grid is
additionally computed only for the inspection plots shown later in this
chapter and plays no role in calibration or training.

Before any HRV measure is computed, the raw R-R interval series recorded
by the Polar H10 is corrected for artifacts using the beat
classification method of Lipponen and Tarvainen [@lipponen2019],
implemented in NeuroKit2 [@makowski2021]. A single misdetected heartbeat
can otherwise distort every downstream HRV value, so correction is
applied per window before the arousal signal is derived.

Valence is derived from facial expressions. Each sampled video frame is
passed through HSEmotion [@savchenko2022], a model trained on the
AffectNet corpus [@mollahosseini2019] that outputs a continuous valence
estimate per detected face. These per-frame estimates are averaged per
window, weighted by the model's own confidence, to obtain a single
valence value for that window.

Arousal is derived from HRV by combining RMSSD with mean heart rate into
a single index. Since RMSSD decreases with physiological activation
while heart rate increases with it [@kreibig2010], RMSSD is inverted
before the two measures are averaged. Both quantities enter this index
as robust z-scores relative to the session's own median and spread.

Because resting heart rate, HRV, and facial expression differ
substantially between individuals, no single threshold could separate an
emotionally salient window from a neutral one across all participants: a
resting heart rate of 90 bpm might indicate heightened activation for
one person and be entirely unremarkable for another. The labeling
algorithm therefore has no fixed notion of "normal"; instead, each
session's own data is used to establish what counts as this
participant's baseline on that day, against which deviations are then
judged.

Both axes are then discretized using the same logic, independently
applied and centered on the participant's own session median. A window
is classified as positive or negative in valence, or as activated or
calm in arousal, when its value lies outside a deadband of
$\tau = k \cdot (1.4826 \cdot \text{MAD})$ around that median; otherwise
it falls into the respective neutral category. Median and MAD are
recomputed independently for each session, from that session's own
non-overlapping 30-second windows introduced above, so that a
participant's individual resting level and spread define the reference
against which their own windows are judged. The constant $k$, by
contrast, is fixed at 0.5 for both axes and was chosen once by
inspecting a real pilot session, rather than being re-estimated per
participant. The two resulting labels are then crossed into the final
emotion label, following the logic of the circumplex model presented by
@russell1980: if either the valence or the arousal label is neutral, the
window is assigned the overall label *neutral*; only if both axes are
non-neutral is the window assigned one of the four directional labels,
*negative activated*, *negative calm*, *positive activated*, or
*positive calm*, formed by combining the non-neutral valence category
(negative/positive) with the non-neutral arousal category
(calm/activated). This crossing rule follows directly from the quadrant
structure of the circumplex model [@russell1980], in which only the four
outer quadrants correspond to a clearly directional affective state,
while any window touching the neutral zone on either axis is treated as
affectively unspecific.

## Feature Engineering

Following on from the field work (Section 4.3), the dataset creation
step automatically turns raw recording sessions into one consolidated,
machine-learning-ready dataset. It first runs the emotion labeling
pipeline (Section 4.4) on every session to (re)generate that session's
labeled windows, then collects and merges the non-overlapping ML-grid
export from each session. The label produced is a proxy label, not
ground truth, and there is no self-report to validate it against
(Section 4.4). This step does not change that. It only automates running
the pipeline across every session and merging the results.

The workflow scans the input directory for all session folders and runs
the emotion labeling pipeline for each session. This produces a CSV file
per session folder, containing non-overlapping windows and one row per
window. Next, it verifies that a labeled CSV was created for each
session. If successful, all labeled CSV files are loaded, checked for an
identical column schema, and merged into one consolidated dataset. After
merging, duplicate windows, which are identified by session ID and
window start time, are removed, and windows the labeling pipeline could
not classify (label "excluded") are dropped by default. The final
consolidated dataset therefore contains only successfully classified,
non-duplicate windows.

## Machine Learning Models

To build a human emotion classifier, we trained and compared three ML
models (RandomForest, NeuralNet, and XGBoost) that predict the arousal,
valence, and emotion label from the plant bioelectric features of each
30-second window, and we then identified the best-performing model. The
procedure is the same for each target variable, except that different
classes are predicted. As an example, the target "arousal level" is one
of the two independent axes generated by the emotion labeling algorithm
(Section 4.4). The other axis, the cross-referenced emotion "label," and
all HRV and FER columns are excluded from the features for the target
variable arousal. Therefore, the model only sees the plant signal,
nothing derived from heart rate or facial data, which also applies to
the other target variables. The plant signal is always the only input
for the ML models. The classes to predict are: arousal (calm, neutral,
activated), valence (negative, neutral, positive), emotion (negative
calm, negative activated, neutral, positive calm, positive activated).

The pipeline for each target variable proceeds as follows. The
consolidated dataset (output from Section 4.5) is loaded and the plant
bioelectrical features are exclusively selected. For each ML model, two
feature representations of the plant data are established and compared:
"raw," i.e. values on an absolute scale, and "session_norm," i.e. a
robust z-score relative to the median of the respective recording
session. This results in six combinations to be compared for each of the
three target variables. The data is cleaned by handling missing values,
encoding categorical variables, and removing redundant columns. The
dataset is grouped by participant and split via a nested, stratified
group k-fold cross-validation (5 outer folds). No participant's windows
ever appear in both the training and test portion of a fold to avoid
participant leakage. Following that, features are scaled where the model
requires it. The neural network is wrapped in a StandardScaler and
classifier pipeline fit fresh inside each fold, while the tree-based
models (Random Forest, XGBoost) are scale-invariant and need no scaling.
Hyperparameter tuning is done via nested grid search and uses a separate
inner cross-validation within each outer fold's training data only. The
ML models are evaluated based on accuracy, f1, ROC-AUC, a confusion
matrix, and a classification report. Based on that, the models are
compared and the feature importance examined (Section 5). Based on the
training process, the best model for each axis is identified based on
the f1 macro score, which is then used in the live dashboard. Therefore,
for every 30-second window, the winning ML model per axis runs on the
window's features.

## Live Demonstration

To demonstrate the whole setup, we developed a single dashboard that
shows every data source at once. This includes the live signals detected
by the sensors (Section 4.2): plant bioelectric voltage, CO~2~, heart
rate, and camera feed. In addition, two values per axis (arousal,
valence, emotion) are calculated and displayed side by side. On the one
hand, it shows the proxy labels, applied live to HRV and FER (based on
the rule presented in Section 4.4). On the other hand, it presents the
corresponding plant-model predictions of arousal, valence, and emotion.
These predictions originate from the three pre-trained ML models,
whereas the best model for each axis is identified based on the f1 macro
score (Section 4.6), which is then used for the live demonstration.
Therefore, for every 30-second window, the winning ML model per axis
runs on the window's features.

Every live signal updates continuously. Only the two predictions per
axis are window-based. Both recompute once every window of data has been
collected. There is no training here; the winning models are only loaded
once. To teach what is "normal" for the participant in the particular
session (e.g. heart rate), the labeling algorithm performs a one-time
calibration based on the entire recorded session and knowing all windows
(Section 4.4). However, the live dashboard has no fixed session end to
batch over, which is why the calibration is recomputed after each
completed window. Therefore, it is growing across the live session and
updates in real time. After each new window, the median and MAD are
recalculated based on all previous windows, and the longer the session
runs, the more stable and accurate the "normal value" becomes. At the
beginning of a session, the classification is therefore less reliable
than later on.

## Correlation Analysis

The correlation analysis is conducted to answer the confounding variable
question of whether CO~2~ explains the plant-valence relationship found
in Section 5.1.1. The analysis examines whether CO~2~ is a common
influencing factor of the plant signal and valence, i.e. a confounding
variable. When a participant's valence changes, their breathing changes,
which in turn alters the CO~2~ concentration in the environment, which
may affect the voltage between the plant and the electrode. If this
correlation does indeed exist, it could mean that the plant tracks
valence solely because CO~2~ influences both factors.

Therefore, we test this as a triangle (plant-valence, plant-CO~2~,
CO~2~-valence) and a partial Spearman correlation
$\rho(\text{plant}, \text{valence} \mid \text{CO}_2)$ as the decisive
test. This is performed across all 22 plant features, evaluated in two
complementary variants: a raw analysis (variance both between and within
sessions) and a session-normalized analysis (variance within-session
only). CO~2~ can only be the explanation if both sides of the CO~2~
pathway hold true: that is, if CO~2~ varies in conjunction with the
plant's characteristics and valence. If either of the two branches is
missing and the analysis reduces the correlation between plant and
valence to nearly zero, CO~2~ is a potential confounding factor and
cannot be the reason why the plant's valence signal changes.
